parts.title: Booking a photography workshop
parts.context: A man phones an arts centre to book a place on a photography workshop.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning an arts centre to book a place on a photography workshop. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Riverside Arts Centre, Karen speaking.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Hello. I'm calling about the photography workshop you advertised. I'd like to book a place, please.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Of course. Is that the beginners' workshop or the advanced one?

script.speaker: sam
script.text: The beginners' one. I only bought my first proper camera last month.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller wants the beginners' workshop, so 'beginners' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Right. The next workshop is on Saturday the fourteenth of June. We normally start at half past nine, but this time it's ten o'clock, because the room isn't free until then. We finish at four.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: That's fine. How much does it cost?

script.speaker: karen
script.text: It's seventy-five pounds, but there's a discount for anyone under twenty-five. Are you under twenty-five?

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Yes, I'm twenty-three.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Then it's sixty-five pounds. That includes lunch in our café and all the printing materials.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Great. Where does it take place? In the main building?

script.speaker: karen
script.text: No, it's in the old mill building at the back of the car park. You'll see a sign. And do bring your camera, of course, and spare batteries, because you'll be taking a lot of pictures.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: I will. Thanks.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Now, can I take your name?

script.speaker: sam
script.text: It's Sam Whitcombe. That's W-H-I-T-C-O-M-B-E.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Thank you, Sam. Can I ask how you heard about the workshop?

script.speaker: sam
script.text: I saw a poster in the library, next to the noticeboard. It looked really interesting.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Good. Lunch is included, as I said. Do you have any special dietary needs?

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Yes, I'm vegetarian, so I'd need a vegetarian option, please.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: No problem. You can pay on the day, but we only take cards, not cash, so please remember to bring one.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Understood. And who's teaching the workshop?

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Marcus Bell. He's a wildlife photographer, so he's very good at explaining how to take pictures of things that won't stay still.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: That sounds perfect. I'm looking forward to it.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A backstage tour of a theatre
parts.context: A guide shows a group round a historic theatre.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a guide giving a backstage tour of a theatre. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Fairfield Theatre. My name's Helen, and I'll be taking you behind the scenes today. Please look at the plan in your guide. We're standing in the foyer, near the bottom of the plan, and we came in through the main entrance. The box office, where you collected your tickets, is on the left.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: On the right-hand side of the foyer, in the corner, is the café. We'll finish the tour there, and I can promise you the cakes are excellent.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Now, let's go through the auditorium towards the stage. The rooms on both sides are for the people who make the shows possible. At the top left, next to the stage, is the costume workshop. It's the biggest room backstage, because a single production can need more than a hundred costumes.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Directly opposite, at the top right of the plan, is the props store, where we keep everything from fake swords to a real sofa. Please don't try to sit on anything.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Down the left side of the auditorium, just below the costume workshop, are the dressing rooms. The actors use them, and they get very crowded on opening night. Below the dressing rooms is the lighting store, but it's far too small for a visit.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Down the right side, below the props store, is the sound studio, where all the sound effects are made, and below the sound studio is the rehearsal room. It's exactly the same size as the stage, so the actors can practise just as they'll perform.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: A little about the building. The Fairfield opened in eighteen ninety-two, and it was one of the first theatres in the country to have electric lighting. The owners were so nervous that it might fail that they kept the gas lamps as a backup for the first ten years.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: During the Second World War, many people think the theatre became a hospital. In fact it was used as a food store, and the stage was piled high with sacks of flour. Performances started again in nineteen forty-nine.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Between two thousand and eighteen and two thousand and twenty-one, the theatre was restored at a cost of four million pounds. The seats were repaired and reused, and the roof needed only small repairs. The biggest job was the stage floor, which was so badly worn that the whole thing had to be replaced.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Now, a few rules. Please stay on the marked path at all times, because some of the stairs are steep and the floor backstage is uneven. You may take photographs, but not with flash, and please don't touch the costumes, as many of them are over a hundred years old.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: At the end of the tour, back in the café, each of you will have a chance to try on a costume from our collection. And if you enjoy today, there's a half-price ticket for tonight's performance, for anyone with a school card. Shall we begin?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A presentation on cycling in cities
parts.context: Two students discuss a presentation on cycling in cities with their tutor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Priya and Tom, talking to their tutor, Dr Okafor, about a presentation on cycling in cities. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: okafor
script.text: Come in, both of you. I've read the outline of your presentation on cycling in cities, and I'd like to talk it through. First, how did you choose the topic?

script.speaker: tom
script.text: I'd wanted to look at transport for a while, but I couldn't decide what to focus on. Then Priya showed me an article about a city that built a hundred kilometres of cycle lanes in one year, and that was it.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: I did think about traffic and pollution, but cycling seemed more positive, and it has some interesting numbers.

script.speaker: okafor
script.text: Good. Now, you say you'll compare cities that have cycle lanes with cities that don't. Where will you get your information?

script.speaker: priya
script.text: Mainly from official statistics. But they only tell us how many people cycle, not why, so we want to do a survey as well.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: We were going to interview students at the university, because it's easy, but Priya thinks it would be better to ask people in the town centre.

script.speaker: okafor
script.text: I agree with Priya. Students are not typical commuters, and your results would be biased. How many people can you interview?

script.speaker: tom
script.text: We've got three weeks, so perhaps eighty people.

script.speaker: okafor
script.text: That's enough for a student project, as long as you ask exactly the same questions each time. Keep the questionnaire short, no more than eight questions.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: We'll put it on a tablet, so we don't need to type anything up afterwards.

script.speaker: okafor
script.text: Sensible. Now, the structure. You've planned three case studies: Amsterdam, Bogotá and Manchester. Is that too much for a fifteen-minute talk?

script.speaker: tom
script.text: We thought so too. We could drop Bogotá, because the data's harder to find.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: But it's the most interesting example, because they close the main roads on Sundays. I'd rather drop Manchester.

script.speaker: okafor
script.text: I'd keep Amsterdam as the model everyone knows, and Bogotá for the contrast. Manchester is the least original, so Priya's right.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: Then we'll have more time for the conclusions.

script.speaker: okafor
script.text: Yes. And think about how you'll finish. Many students end with a long list of facts, which is dull. Finish on one clear recommendation instead.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: okafor
script.text: Let's go through the sections one by one. The introduction is excellent. It's short, it states your question in one sentence, and it's very clear.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: Thank you. We weren't sure about the part with the cycle-lane map.

script.speaker: okafor
script.text: A map is a good idea, but at the moment you describe the routes in words, and nobody will follow that. You need a picture of the lanes on the slide.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: And the section on costs?

script.speaker: okafor
script.text: That's too technical. You use terms like 'marginal benefit', and most of the audience won't know them. Say it in plain language.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: What about our claim that cycle lanes make streets safer?

script.speaker: okafor
script.text: At the moment it's based on one city. You need more evidence, such as figures from at least two others, before you can say that.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: And the final section, about the future of cycling?

script.speaker: okafor
script.text: It's interesting, but it's right at the end, when people are tired. I'd move it to the start of the talk, just after the introduction, because it will make people curious.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: That makes sense. We'll send you a new draft on Friday.

script.speaker: okafor
script.text: Good. I look forward to reading it.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the history of tea
parts.context: A lecture on the history of tea, from legend to the tea bag.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of tea. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today I'm going to talk about the history of tea, which is the most widely drunk manufactured drink in the world, apart from water.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: According to legend, tea was discovered in China, when leaves from a wild tree blew into a pot of boiling water belonging to an emperor. Whether or not that is true, we know that by the seventh century, in the Tang dynasty, tea was being grown, traded and written about. At that time it was pressed into hard bricks, which were broken up and boiled, often with salt.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Tea reached Japan with Buddhist monks, who found that it helped them stay awake during long periods of meditation. By the twelfth century they had developed a powdered form, called matcha, which is whisked in water rather than soaked.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: European traders first brought tea home in the early sixteen hundreds. The Dutch came first, but it was the British who made it a national habit. At first it was so expensive that it was kept in locked boxes, and the lady of the house kept the key. Heavy taxes made it more expensive still, and by the late seventeen hundreds most of the tea drunk in Britain had been smuggled.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The East India Company controlled the legal trade, and it had a problem. It was buying tea from China, but the Chinese wanted silver as payment, not British goods. So the Company began to grow tea in India instead. The first plantations were started in the eighteen thirties, in the north-eastern region of Assam, using a local variety of the plant that was quite different from the Chinese one.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Meanwhile, speed mattered. Fast sailing ships called clippers raced to bring the first tea of each season back to London, and the winning captain received a prize. These races came to an end when the Suez Canal opened in eighteen sixty-nine, because steamships could use the canal and sailing ships could not.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Finally, the tea bag. It was invented by accident in nineteen oh eight, by a merchant in New York who sent samples to his customers in small silk bags. The customers assumed they were supposed to put the whole bag into the pot, and soon they were asking for more of them.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So, to summarise: a legend, some monks, a smuggling problem, a race and a mistake. Next week we'll look at coffee, which has an equally surprising history.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
